questions.question: What is the Requests library, and how do you make GET and POST requests in Python?
questions.title: Python Requests: GET, POST, and Response Objects
questions.direct_answer: Requests is a third-party Python package for sending HTTP requests. Use requests.get() to retrieve a representation and requests.post() to submit data. Both return a Response object; production code should set a timeout, check the HTTP result, and only then decode the body.

interviewer_intent.testing: HTTP method choice, request construction, Response handling, and timeout discipline.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling Requests part of the Python standard library or treating every returned Response as success.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish params=, json=, and data= and explain that HTTP errors need an explicit status policy.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Requests is a third-party package, not part of Python's standard library.
requests.get(url, params=...) sends a GET request; requests.post(url, json=...) sends a JSON body.
A Response exposes status_code, headers, content, text, and json().
Call raise_for_status() when a non-2xx/3xx response should become an exception.
Always choose a timeout; Requests has no default timeout.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Requests is a third-party Python package that makes synchronous HTTP client code easier to read. A GET asks for a resource representation, while a POST submits data for the server to process, often to create a resource or start an action. Requests simplifies the call syntax but does not change those HTTP meanings.

Use `requests.get(url, params={...}, timeout=...)` for a GET with query parameters. Requests safely encodes the names and values and appends them to the URL. The returned `Response` is separate from the request and contains the status, headers, raw bytes, decoded text, and helpers for common body formats.

Use `json={"name": "Ada"}` when the endpoint expects a JSON body. Requests serializes the dictionary and supplies the JSON content type. Use `data=...` for form fields or a deliberately prepared raw body. The API documentation decides which form is correct; the arguments are not interchangeable just because each accepts Python values.

A `404` or `500` is still an HTTP response, so Requests normally returns a `Response` for it. Call `raise_for_status()` when those statuses should stop the operation, or branch on an expected status deliberately. Only then decode the body with `json()`, `text`, or `content` and validate the value your application needs.

Production code still needs explicit timeouts, transport-error handling, an endpoint-specific status policy, and data validation. POST should not be retried blindly because the first attempt may already have created an effect. Requests removes repetitive HTTP plumbing; the application still owns method choice, recovery, and the meaning of the returned data.

sections.title: From Python values to a checked HTTP response
sections.content:
An API call crosses two boundaries. First, Python values must become an HTTP request: method, URL, headers, and possibly a body. Then an HTTP response must become an application value. Requests helps with both conversions, but it does not decide whether the result is correct for the business operation.

params= percent-encodes query values and attaches them to the URL. json= serializes a Python value and supplies an application/json content type. data= is used for form-style fields or raw request data. These arguments are not interchangeable simply because all of them accept Python values.

On the return path, inspect the status before trusting the body. raise_for_status() is convenient when every client or server error should stop the operation, but some programs intentionally branch on statuses such as 404. json() only decodes the bytes; it does not prove that required fields exist or have the expected types.

A timeout is part of correctness, not just performance. Without one, a stalled peer can hold a worker for an unbounded time. A useful client therefore makes the timeout and error policy visible near the call.

sections.title: From Python values to a checked response
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Python values] --> B[Requests builds method, URL, headers, body]
  B --> S[HTTP server]
  S --> R[Response: status, headers, bytes]
  R --> C{Status acceptable?}
  C -->|yes| D[Decode and validate body]
  C -->|no| E[Handle or raise HTTPError]
```

sections.title: Worked Python example
sections.content:
```python
import requests

def fetch_active_users(base_url: str) -> list[dict]:
    response = requests.get(
        f"{base_url}/users",
        params={"active": "true"},
        timeout=(3.05, 10),
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    payload = response.json()
    if not isinstance(payload, list):
        raise ValueError("users response must be a JSON array")
    return payload

def create_user(base_url: str, name: str) -> dict:
    response = requests.post(
        f"{base_url}/users",
        json={"name": name},
        timeout=(3.05, 10),
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()
```

questions.question: When should you use Python Requests instead of urllib.request?
questions.title: Requests vs urllib.request
questions.direct_answer: Use Requests when a project can add a dependency and benefits from a clearer API for sessions, authentication, JSON bodies, cookies, and response handling. Use urllib.request when adding dependencies is undesirable and the HTTP work is small enough that the lower-level standard-library interface is acceptable.

interviewer_intent.testing: The dependency and ergonomics trade-off between Requests and urllib.request.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming Requests changes HTTP semantics or is always preferable regardless of dependency constraints.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the choice to client complexity, dependency policy, and synchronous execution.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Requests is third-party; urllib.request ships with Python.
Requests has a smaller, more convenient API for common HTTP client work.
urllib.request is useful in dependency-restricted scripts or libraries.
Both still require explicit timeouts, status handling, and response validation.
Choose for project constraints, not because one library changes HTTP semantics.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Requests and `urllib.request` can both make HTTP calls. Requests is an installed third-party package with a concise API for query parameters, JSON, sessions, cookies, authentication, and responses. `urllib.request` ships with Python and exposes lower-level standard-library building blocks. Neither one changes the remote API's behavior.

Use Requests when the project can add a dependency and the client makes several authenticated or JSON calls. A `requests.Session` can keep shared headers, cookies, and connection reuse in one place. Its `params`, `json`, and `Response` APIs usually make application code shorter and easier to review.

Use `urllib.request` for a small script, reusable library, or restricted environment where adding a dependency is not worthwhile. A one-call health check may need only `urlopen()` and a timeout. As authentication, sessions, JSON bodies, or repeated calls grow, the extra manual code can become harder to maintain than the dependency it avoided.

Both libraries need timeouts, TLS verification, status handling, safe retry rules, logging, and response validation. Requests is not automatically safer, and `urllib.request` is not automatically lighter once a project rebuilds sessions and helpers around it. Highly concurrent async code should compare an async HTTP client instead of forcing either synchronous API into that design.

The complete example prepares the same encoded GET with both libraries and sends no traffic. Requests accepts the query dictionary directly, while the standard-library version uses `urlencode` and `Request`. The final URL is the same; the difference is how much client-side setup the project wants to own.

Requests is an installed third-party package with a concise API for query parameters, JSON, sessions, cookies, authentication, and responses. `urllib.request` ships with Python and exposes lower-level standard-library building blocks. Neither one changes the remote API's behavior.

A `requests.Session` can keep shared headers, cookies, and connection reuse in one place. Its `params`, `json`, and `Response` APIs usually make application code shorter and easier to review.

sections.title: Dependency cost and HTTP client complexity
sections.content:
The two libraries differ mainly in ergonomics and packaging. urllib.request exposes standard-library building blocks such as Request and urlopen. Requests wraps common HTTP operations in higher-level objects and consistent keyword arguments.

A dependency has a cost: it must be pinned, updated, and included in deployment and security maintenance. That cost is often small compared with the duplicated code avoided in a real API client. In a reusable library with a strict dependency budget, the balance may reverse.

Neither option is a universal production client by itself. A service still needs a clear policy for timeouts, retries, observability, TLS verification, status codes, and schema validation. Concurrency is a separate decision as both APIs in this comparison are synchronous.

sections.title: Choose by constraint
sections.content:
| Concern | Requests | urllib.request |
|---|---|---|
| Installation | Third-party dependency | Python standard library |
| Common JSON API calls | Concise helpers and Response API | More manual request/response work |
| Sessions and cookies | Session abstraction | Build with lower-level handlers |
| Best fit | Application API clients | Small dependency-free tasks |
| Async support | No | No |

sections.title: Worked Python example
sections.content:
```python
# Both examples prepare the same GET without sending network traffic.
import requests
from urllib.parse import urlencode
from urllib.request import Request

prepared = requests.Request(
    "GET", "https://example.com/search", params={"q": "python http"}
).prepare()
assert prepared.url == "https://example.com/search?q=python+http"

query = urlencode({"q": "python http"})
standard_request = Request(f"https://example.com/search?{query}", method="GET")
assert standard_request.full_url == prepared.url
```

questions.question: What mistakes should you avoid when reading a Requests response?
questions.title: Safely Reading a Requests Response
questions.direct_answer: Do not assume that receiving a Response means the operation succeeded or that its body is valid JSON. Check the expected status, handle HTTP and transport failures separately, inspect the content type when useful, decode the body once, and validate the resulting shape before using its fields.

interviewer_intent.testing: The order of status, representation, and application-shape checks.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling response.json() before dealing with an error status or assuming decoded JSON is a dictionary.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate a 502 HTML body, malformed JSON, and a valid payload with an invalid schema.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A 4xx or 5xx response is returned normally until raise_for_status() is called.
response.json() can fail when the body is empty, HTML, or malformed JSON.
Successful JSON decoding does not validate required keys or value types.
Use content for bytes and text for decoded text; do not guess for binary data.
Keep error-body logging small and redact secrets or personal data.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Requests `Response` proves that an HTTP response arrived. It does not prove that the operation succeeded or that the body has the expected data. A `404` and `500` are responses too. Start with the endpoint's expected status rule instead of immediately reading fields from the body.

Call `raise_for_status()` when every unsuccessful status should become `HTTPError`, or branch on an expected status such as `404` when it has normal meaning. A gateway may return `502` with an HTML error page; trying `response.json()` first hides the more useful HTTP failure behind a JSON error.

A successful `204 No Content` response normally has no body, so JSON decoding is the wrong next step. When a body is expected, use `content` for bytes, `text` for decoded text, and `json()` for JSON. Content type is useful evidence, but the endpoint contract still defines what should arrive.

`response.json()` may return a dictionary, list, string, number, Boolean, or `None`. It checks JSON syntax, not required fields. If a profile function promises a dictionary with an integer `id`, check that exact shape before returning it instead of allowing later code to fail with an unrelated key or type error.

For a failed response, record useful details such as method, safe URL context, status, attempt count, and server request ID. Keep body samples small and remove tokens, personal data, and secrets. The practical rule is status first, expected body second, decoder third, and field validation last.

A `404` and `500` are responses too. Start with the endpoint's expected status rule instead of immediately reading fields from the body.

When a body is expected, use `content` for bytes, `text` for decoded text, and `json()` for JSON. Content type is useful evidence, but the endpoint contract still defines what should arrive.

sections.title: Response handling as a validation pipeline
sections.content:
Response handling is a pipeline with different failure meanings. A DNS failure happens before any response exists. A 500 response is valid HTTP describing server failure. A JSON decoding error says the received bytes are not the representation the decoder expected. A missing field means decoding worked but the application contract did not.

Keeping these layers separate produces clearer recovery. A retry policy may apply to a transient transport failure or 503, but it will not repair a permanent schema mismatch. Likewise, catching every RequestException around JSON and validation code can blur the true cause.

Content-Type is useful evidence, although real APIs are sometimes misconfigured. The most reliable client combines status rules, an expected media type, careful decoding, and explicit checks for the shape it actually needs.

sections.title: Response checks in the right order
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Response arrived] --> B{Expected status?}
  B -->|no| C[Handle status or raise]
  B -->|yes| D{Body expected?}
  D -->|no, such as 204| E[Finish without decoding]
  D -->|yes| F[Decode bytes or JSON]
  F --> G[Validate fields and types]
```
